**Chapter 8: Chemistry and Energy**

**8.1 Electrolysis of Concentrate Sodium Chloride Solution**

In concentrated sodium chloride solution, NaCl becomes ionized and produces Na+ and Cl- ions.

The difference from molten sodium chloride is that the solution contains H+ and OH- ions too as water is partially ionized here.

During the electrolysis in this electrolytic cell, Na+ and H+ will go towards the cathode together. We know, H+ ion is more prone to accept electrons than the Na+ ion. So, H+ ion accepts one electron at the cathode and becomes a H atom. Two H atoms again join together and become a H2 molecule. The reaction at the cathode:

H+ + e- → H (Reduction reaction)

H + H → H2

Cl- and OH- go simultaneously towards the anode. We know, OH- ion is more prone to donate an electron than Cl-. However, since the molarity of Cl- in the solution is higher than OH-, so it donates electrons at the anode earlier than OH-. One Cl- ion donates an electron at the anode and becomes a Cl atom. Two Cl atoms join together producing a Cl2 molecule. The reaction at the anode:

Cl- → Cl + e- (Oxidation)

Cl + Cl → Cl2

**8.2 Conclusion**

In conclusion, the electrolysis of concentrate sodium chloride solution produces hydrogen gas and chlorine gas. The reaction at the cathode is:

H+ + e- → H (Reduction reaction)

H + H → H2

The reaction at the anode is:

Cl- → Cl + e- (Oxidation)

Cl + Cl → Cl2

(a) The solution contains H+ and OH- ions too as water is partially ionized here.
(b) The solution does not contain H+ and OH- ions.
(c) The solution contains only Na+ and Cl- ions.
(d) The solution contains only H+ and OH- ions.

(b) H + H → H2
